newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian parliament rejects draft law on elections.
newsitem.headline: Italian parliament rejects draft law on elections.

text.p: Parliament on Thursday rejected a legislative proposal which opposition parties had said would help open the way to deep electoral reform in Italy.
The Chamber of Deputies (lower house) voted by 261 to 248 against the proposal, submitted by a member of centre-right opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi's Forza Italia party.

Opposition politicians had billed the vote as a test of parliament's commitment to changing Italy's political system, the subject of negotiations now under way by a special commission of both houses on constitutional reform.
"This is how all reforms will be done now," the proposal's sponsor, Giorgio Rebuffa, said after the vote.
Rebuffa's proposal was a technical measure designed to overcome constitutional objections that have so far prevented steps to put the issue of electoral reform to a referendum.

The Constitutional Court this month rejected a petition for a referendum to abolish the remaining element of proportional representation (PR) in Italy's electoral system, ruling that a vote to scrap PR would create a legislative void.
To overcome the objections, Rebuffa had proposed allowing existing electoral law to remain on the statute books, even if rejected in a referendum, until parliament had passed a new law.
Many of the votes against came from small parties in parliament on both sides of the divide which would almost certainly lose their seats if Italy were to move to a straight majority voting system.

"They want to destroy the communists by law, seeing as they haven't been able to do it politically," said Oliviero Diliberto, whose hard left Communist Refoundation party ensures the centre-left government's majority in parliament.
Italy had pure proportional representation until a referendum in 1993 showed an overwhelming desire for political change following huge corruption scandals.
The subsequent reform created a system by which 75 percent of seats in parliament are awarded by majority voting and the remainder by proportional representation.
Public opinion polls show most Italians would like a straight majority voting system.
